label: Jul 6, 2026
headline: US visa wait times hit new highs at Indian consulates — Mumbai at 10 months, Kolkata nearly doubles to 7 months
summary: The State Department's July 2026 wait time data reveals further deterioration across all five Indian consulates. Mumbai B1/B2 waits have hit 300 days (10 months), the longest nationally. New Delhi jumped to 255 days (8.5 months), up from 7.5 months in June. Kolkata — previously the fastest option at 4 months — has surged to 210 days (7 months), nearly doubling in weeks. Hyderabad holds at 285 days (9.5 months). Chennai shows no interview availability at all, with only dropbox processing listed. Work visa (H/L/O/P/Q) waits remain 45–105 days depending on the consulate, and student visa (F/M/J) waits are 45–60 days. The continued surge comes despite the State Department's $750 premium interview pilot launching July 1, which offers B1/B2 applicants expedited appointments within 10 business days at select posts. Participating locations have not yet been announced for India. With the USCIS signature rule also taking effect July 10 — potentially causing denials for digital-signature filings — Indian visa applicants face a convergence of new pressures heading into the second half of 2026.
source: US State Department / travel.state.gov / afnovisaguide.com

label: Jul 1, 2026
headline: Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship 6-3 — strikes down Trump executive order as unconstitutional
summary: In a landmark ruling on the final day of its term, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's executive order that sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born in the US to non-citizen parents. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for a five-member majority, held that the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause — granting citizenship to all persons born on US soil and "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" — cannot be overridden by executive action, citing the 1898 precedent United States v. Wong Kim Ark. Justice Kavanaugh concurred on statutory grounds, suggesting Congress could legislate changes but the president cannot act alone. The ruling is especially significant for Indian families navigating years-long green card backlogs on H-1B, H-4, L-1, and other temporary visas, where children are frequently born in the US long before their parents obtain permanent residency. Trump called the decision "too bad for our country" and urged Congress to pass legislation ending birthright citizenship — a move that would face even steeper constitutional hurdles.
source: US Supreme Court (Trump v. Barbara) / NBC News / Brookings / Reuters

label: Jun 30, 2026
headline: USCIS signature crackdown takes effect July 10 — DocuSign and digital shortcuts may trigger denials on H-1B and green card filings
summary: An interim final rule published May 11 in the Federal Register takes effect July 10, 2026, giving USCIS explicit authority to deny — not just reject — immigration benefit requests with invalid signatures. Unlike a rejection (which refunds fees), a denial means the agency keeps the filing fee and the petitioner must start over. Affected filings include H-1B petitions, L-1 transfers, I-140 green card petitions, and I-485 adjustment of status applications. Prohibited formats now include DocuSign, Adobe Sign, copy-pasted digital signature images, rubber stamps, and typed names — only wet-ink signatures, scanned copies of wet-ink originals, and electronic signatures within USCIS-authorized online systems are accepted. Immigration attorneys warn USCIS may increasingly choose denial over rejection since denial lets the agency retain fees. Employers and HR teams using remote or digital signing workflows — common in the Indian IT sector — should audit their practices immediately before the July 10 deadline.
source: USCIS / Federal Register / Holland & Hart / Ogletree Deakins

label: Jun 27, 2026
headline: US tourist visa wait times surge up to 36% at Indian consulates — Hyderabad and Mumbai now at 9.5 months
summary: The State Department's June 18 global wait time update reveals a sharp spike in B1/B2 visitor visa interview waits at Indian posts. Hyderabad and Mumbai now average 9.5 months (next available: 9.5 and 10 months respectively), up from ~7 months a month earlier — among the longest globally. New Delhi climbed to 7.5 months avg (8.5 next available), up from 5.5 months. Chennai held at 5.5 months. Kolkata is the lone bright spot, improving to 4 months. The surge is attributed to expanded social media and digital footprint screening protocols in effect since December 15, 2025, which have slashed daily interview capacity and triggered mass appointment rescheduling — often pushing slots 90 to 120 days later. Work visa (H/L/O/P/Q) waits remain far shorter at 1.5–3.5 months, and student visa (F/M/J) waits are 1.5–2 months. With the $750 premium interview pilot launching July 1, India's consulates are among the most likely participating posts given the severity of their backlogs.
source: US State Department / travel.state.gov / Bhasha Times

label: Jun 22, 2026
headline: White House clears rule to end 'Duration of Status' — US student visas to get fixed expiry dates, 4-year cap
summary: The White House's Office of Management and Budget has completed its review of a DHS proposal that would scrap the decades-old 'Duration of Status' (D/S) framework for F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors and certain I (foreign media) visa holders, replacing it with fixed admission periods capped at four years. Under D/S, students could stay as long as they remained enrolled and compliant, with no fixed end date; the new rule sets a hard expiry and requires applicants to file an extension of stay with USCIS to continue beyond it. With OMB clearance done, the rule is expected to be published in the Federal Register and move toward implementation later this year. Indian students — the largest international cohort in the US at ~363,000 in 2024-25 — are among the most affected, especially those in PhD, research-heavy or other multi-year programs that run past four years, who will now face extension filings, added documentation and biometrics, shorter post-completion grace periods (proposed cut from 60 to 30 days), and stricter rules on transferring schools or changing programs.
source: DHS / OMB / Times of India / India Today

label: Jun 19, 2026
headline: US to revive domestic H-1B visa renewal pilot in December — ~20,000 slots, mostly for Indians
summary: Julie Stufft, Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Visa Services, confirmed the US will launch a domestic visa renewal pilot for certain H-1B holders starting December, allowing eligible workers already inside the US to renew without traveling abroad for a consular interview. The State Department will issue about 20,000 visas over the first three months, and Stufft said the 'vast majority' will go to Indian nationals — the largest skilled-worker group in the US — with plans to expand. She acknowledged India's 6-to-12-month interview wait times are 'not what we need,' and said the program will free up US missions in India to focus on first-time applicants. A Federal Register notice with eligibility rules and application steps is expected soon. The move, flagged in the recent India-US joint statement and welcomed by the diaspora, revives the domestic revalidation concept first piloted in early 2024.
source: US State Department (Julie Stufft) / The Indian Eye / EY

headline: July 2026 Visa Bulletin: EB-2 India now fully unavailable, EB-1 retrogresses further — green card squeeze deepens
summary: The State Department’s July 2026 Visa Bulletin delivers another blow to Indian employment-based green card applicants. EB-2 India is now marked “Unavailable” — no visas will be issued in this category for the rest of FY2026 (the quota was exhausted in May). EB-1 India retrogressed two more months to October 15, 2022, from December 15, 2022 in June. EB-5 unreserved India is also “Unavailable” after the cap was reached June 5. The only bright spot: EB-3 India inched forward half a month to January 1, 2014. USCIS confirmed that employment-based applicants must use Final Action Dates (not Dates for Filing) to determine I-485 eligibility, further limiting who can file. The State Department warned that additional retrogressions — or more categories going “Unavailable” — are possible before the fiscal year ends September 30. Visa numbers reset October 1 with FY2027.
source: US State Department / July 2026 Visa Bulletin

label: Jun 12, 2026
headline: Court stays $100K H-1B fee ruling — fee remains in effect while First Circuit reviews appeal
summary: Four days after striking down the $100,000 H-1B fee as an unlawful tax, Judge Sorokin granted the government’s request to stay his own order while the Trump administration appeals to the First Circuit Court of Appeals. The stay means USCIS can continue collecting the fee on all new H-1B petitions requiring consular processing. Employers must plan as if the fee is fully enforceable. The DOJ argued that every day without the fee, more workers would “rush to seek H-1B classification,” undermining the policy’s purpose. Parallel challenges to the fee are pending in California and D.C. federal courts; legal experts expect the Supreme Court will ultimately weigh in. The fee’s fate remains deeply uncertain, but for now, it’s back in force.
source: US District Court (D. Mass.) / Bloomberg Law / WR Immigration

Acting AG Todd Blanche said the DOJ now maintains a 'zero-tolerance policy' for abuse of the naturalization process. Denaturalization, averaging just 11 cases/year from 1990-2017, is being sharply expanded — a direct warning to naturalized Indian citizens who obtained status through visa or immigration misrepresentation.

label: May 22, 2026
headline: USCIS declares adjustment of status 'extraordinary relief' — green card applicants directed to leave US and process at consulates abroad
summary: USCIS issued Policy Memorandum PM-602-0199 declaring that adjustment of status (AOS) — the process by which immigrants apply for green cards from inside the US — will now be treated as 'extraordinary' discretionary relief granted only in limited cases. The agency directed officers to consider consular processing abroad as the default pathway, stating temporary visa holders 'must return to their home country to apply, except in extraordinary circumstances.' While eligibility rules have not technically changed and dual-intent visa holders (H-1B, L-1) may still file AOS, the memo instructs adjudicators to apply heightened discretionary review — meaning increased Requests for Evidence, Notices of Intent to Deny, and longer processing times. The policy represents a sharp break from decades of practice where eligible H-1B and L-1 workers routinely adjusted status domestically. For Indian applicants already facing decade-long green card backlogs and 10+ month consular interview waits, being pushed to consular processing could add years of additional delay and force workers to leave their US jobs during the application process. Legal challenges are expected.
source: USCIS PM-602-0199 / Mondaq / Lexology / USA TODAY
